title: Riviera model with egoistical settlers
abstract: The Riviera model mimics a densifying settlement along the coastline. In the lattice version, houses are built sequentially in empty sites with the constraint that every newly built house has at least one empty neighboring site. The distribution of clusters of adjacent houses does not obey a closed set of evolutionary equations, but the void-cluster-void distribution does. We compute the latter and extract the cluster distribution from it. In the jammed state, when all voids have length one and the evolution ceases, the cluster distribution has a neat form and exhibits a factorial decay with the length of the cluster. To investigate finite systems, we employ a static approach directly treating jammed states. If the coastline is a finite segment, we determine the statistics of the number of empty sites in the jammed state (the average, variance, and higher cumulants). We also study a continuum version in which houses are built along the line so that each newly built house is sufficiently separated from at least one neighboring house.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes the statistical mechanics of the Riviera model, a 1D process mimicking constrained settlement. It derives exact formulas for the cluster size distribution and correlation functions in the jammed state by solving complex differential equations. The work provides deep insights into how local constraints dictate global structural properties in disordered systems.
main_problem: The primary goal is characterizing the jammed state of a one-dimensional settlement model (Riviera model) and deriving its cluster size distribution and correlation functions.
main_result: In the jammed state, the cluster size distribution follows an exact factorial decay ($\Pi_s \propto 1/(s+2)!$), and the average number of empty sites in a finite segment scales linearly with length ($L/3 + 1/3$).
method: The analysis employs dynamic evolution equations for void densities, solved using exponential ansatzes, alongside static combinatorial methods for calculating correlation functions.
model_or_system: The Riviera model (RM) simulates densifying settlement on a line segment. It is analyzed in both discrete and continuum forms, involving parameters like the separation threshold $\epsilon$.

important_parameters: The parameter $\epsilon$ governs the generalization of the model; key regimes include $\epsilon=0$, $\epsilon=1$, and the maximum entropy density $ho^*$.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on exponential ansatzes to solve infinite sets of coupled differential equations, and approximations are made when calculating higher-order correlations.

paper_structure: The paper progresses from analyzing the dynamic evolution of void patterns (using ODEs and ansatzes) to determining the exact cluster size distribution in the jammed state. It then extends to calculating pair correlation functions ($C_j$) and finally tackles finite-size statistics using generating functions and continuum limits.
why_interesting: The mathematical techniques used—solving complex, infinite sets of coupled differential equations via ansatzes—are highly relevant for modeling non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body systems, analogous to those studied in quantum field theory or open quantum systems.
